title: Spring Boot essentials
subtitle: Create a project and understand what Spring manages.
description: Create a project with Spring Initializr, run it with Maven Wrapper, and learn how Spring creates beans and connects dependencies. Organize controllers, services, and repositories, then configure each environment.

lessons.title: JDK, Maven & your first project
lessons.summary: Use Java 21 and Maven Wrapper to create and run a consistent Spring Boot project.
objectives: Create a project with Spring Initializr.
Run Maven lifecycle phases through the wrapper.
keyPoints: The examples use Java 21 and Spring Boot 3-style configuration.
Maven Wrapper pins the Maven version used locally and in CI.
SpringBootApplication enables configuration and component scanning.
practice: Create an Initializr project with Spring Web, Validation, and Actuator, then run it.
The application starts and /actuator/health returns UP.

exercises.prompt: What is the main advantage of ./mvnw over a globally installed mvn?
options: Developers and CI use the Maven version pinned by the project.
Builds automatically run twice as fast.
A JDK is no longer required.
exercises.explanation: The wrapper configuration records the Maven version, reducing differences between development and CI.
Running a lifecycle phase also runs the earlier phases. package therefore includes compile and test.

exercises.prompt: Which annotation belongs on the main Spring Boot application class?
exercises.hint: It combines configuration, auto-configuration, and component scanning.
exercises.explanation: @SpringBootApplication enables auto-configuration and scans the main class’s package and its subpackages.

lessons.title: IoC container & constructor injection
lessons.summary: Spring creates and connects objects called beans. Constructors state which dependencies a bean needs.
objectives: Receive required dependencies through a constructor.
Avoid mutable per-request fields in singleton beans.
keyPoints: A single constructor does not need Autowired.
Singleton beans are shared, so request-specific data belongs in local variables or parameters.
practice: Make OrderService a bean with a constructor-injected OrderRepository.
A unit test can create it with new OrderService(fakeRepository).

exercises.prompt: Register OrderService as a Spring bean and inject OrderRepository through its constructor rather than a field.
checks: Annotate the class with Service or Component
Do not use Autowired field injection
exercises.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and allows ordinary Java construction in tests.

exercises.prompt: A Service bean stores currentOrder in a field and assigns it for each request. What is the risk?
options: A shared singleton can overwrite or expose one user’s data to another request.
None; Spring creates a new service for every request.
Spring automatically makes the field thread-safe.
exercises.explanation: Keep request-specific state in local variables or method arguments. A singleton service is shared by concurrent callers.

lessons.title: Controller, service & repository
lessons.summary: The controller handles HTTP, the service coordinates business behavior, and the repository accesses data.
objectives: Map an HTTP route to a controller method.
Keep business rules out of transport code.
Test service behavior without a web server.
keyPoints: RestController writes return values to the response body.
Service/domain rules should also work for messaging and scheduled jobs.
Repositories encapsulate data access rather than business decisions.
practice: Build GET /greetings/{name} backed by a GreetingService.
The endpoint returns a greeting and the service can be tested independently.

exercises.prompt: Complete the controller so GET /greetings/{name} returns service.greet(name).
checks: Use PathVariable on the name parameter
exercises.explanation: The controller adapts HTTP to the service. Greeting behavior stays testable without starting a server.

exercises.prompt: Where should the rule “orders above Rp10 million require manager approval” live?
options: In the service or Order domain object, because it is a business rule.
Only in the controller, because it receives requests.
In the repository while saving the order.
exercises.explanation: Business rules belong in service/domain code so HTTP clients, message consumers, and jobs use the same behavior.

lessons.title: Configuration & profiles
lessons.summary: Run the same JAR in different environments by supplying configuration from files, environment variables, and arguments.
objectives: Keep passwords and tokens outside the repository.
keyPoints: Command-line arguments override environment variables and ordinary config files.
Relaxed binding maps environment variable names to property names.
Profiles group environment-specific behavior; secrets should come from outside the image.
practice: Bind inventory.base-url and inventory.timeout to InventoryProperties and override them through environment variables.
The same JAR uses different values without a rebuild.

exercises.prompt: application.yml sets port 8080, SERVER_PORT is 9090, and startup arguments include --server.port=7070. Which port is used?
options: Startup fails because the values conflict.
exercises.explanation: In this simplified precedence order, command-line arguments override environment variables, which override the packaged config file.

exercises.prompt: Write the environment variable name for spring.datasource.url.
exercises.hint: Use uppercase letters and replace dots with underscores.
exercises.explanation: Relaxed binding maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url.

exercises.prompt: Create InventoryProperties as a record bound to prefix inventory, with String baseUrl and Duration timeout.
exercises.explanation: Register the record with EnableConfigurationProperties or ConfigurationPropertiesScan so it can be injected as a bean.
